Any person operating an aircraft who wishes to receive air traffic services referred to in section 801.24 in English or French shall make their request known to the appropriate ATS unit by means of an initial radiocommunication in English or French.

Subject to sections 602.137 and 602.138, where an aircraft is equipped with radiocommunication equipment, the pilot-in-command shall ensure that
a listening watch is maintained on the appropriate frequency; and
where communications are required, communication is established with an air traffic services unit or community aerodrome radio station, as applicable, on that appropriate frequency.

Where there is a two-way radiocommunication failure between the controlling air traffic control unit and an IFR aircraft that is in or has received a clearance to enter controlled airspace, the pilot-in-command shall
maintain a listening watch on the appropriate frequency for control messages or further clearance and acknowledge receipt of any such messages, if possible, by any means available;
set the transponder to code 7600; and

attempt to establish communications with any air traffic services facility or other aircraft, inform the facility or aircraft of the difficulty and request it to relay the information to the last air traffic control unit with which communications had been established.

Where communications cannot be established with any air traffic services facility, either directly or by relay through an intermediary, the pilot-in-command shall, except where specific instructions to cover an anticipated communications failure have been received from an air traffic control unit, comply with the procedures specified by the Minister in the Canada Air Pilot and the Canada Flight Supplement.

Where there is a two-way radiocommunication failure between the controlling air traffic control unit and a VFR aircraft while operating in Class B, Class C or Class D airspace, the pilot-in-command shall
leave the airspace
where the airspace is a control zone, by landing at the aerodrome for which the control zone is established, and
in any other case, by the shortest route;
where the aircraft is equipped with a transponder, set the transponder to code 7600; and
inform an air traffic control unit as soon as possible of the actions taken pursuant to paragraph (a).
No person shall operate an aircraft equipped with two-way VHF radiocommunication equipment unless the equipment is capable of providing communication on VHF frequency 121.5 MHz.
No person shall give an interception signal or an instruction to land except
a peace officer, an officer of a police authority or an officer of the Canadian Armed Forces acting within the scope of their duties; or
a person authorized to do so by the Minister pursuant to subsection (2).
The Minister may authorize a person to give an interception signal or an instruction to land if such authorization is in the public interest and is not likely to affect aviation safety.

The pilot-in-command of an aircraft who receives an instruction to land from a person referred to in subsection (1) shall, subject to any direction received from an air traffic control unit, comply with the instruction.
The pilot-in-command of an intercepting aircraft and the pilot-in-command of an intercepted aircraft shall comply with the rules of interception set out in the Canada Flight Supplement.
This section applies in respect of aircraft before entering into and while operating within the ADIZ, the dimensions of which are specified in the Designated Airspace Handbook.
Every flight plan or flight itinerary required to be filed pursuant to this section shall be filed with an air traffic services unit or a community aerodrome radio station.

The pilot-in-command of an aircraft whose point of departure within the ADIZ or last point of departure before entering the ADIZ has facilities for the transmission of flight plan or flight itinerary information shall
before take-off, file a flight plan or flight itinerary;
in the case of a VFR aircraft where the point of departure is outside the ADIZ,
indicate in the flight plan or flight itinerary the estimated time and point of ADIZ entry, and

as soon as possible after take-off, communicate by radio to an air traffic control unit, a flight service station or a community aerodrome radio station a position report of the aircraft’s location, altitude, aerodrome of departure and estimated time and point of ADIZ entry; and

in the case of a VFR aircraft where the point of departure is within the ADIZ, as soon as possible after take-off, communicate by radio to an air traffic control unit, a flight service station or a community aerodrome radio station a position report of the aircraft’s location, altitude and aerodrome of departure.

The pilot-in-command of an aircraft whose point of departure within the ADIZ or last point of departure before entering the ADIZ does not have facilities for the transmission of flight plan or flight itinerary information shall
as soon as possible after take-off, file by radiocommunication a flight plan or flight itinerary; and
in the case of a VFR aircraft, indicate in the flight plan or flight itinerary the estimated time and point of ADIZ entry, if applicable.

The pilot-in-command of a VFR aircraft shall revise the estimated time and point of ADIZ entry and inform an air traffic control unit, a flight service station or a community aerodrome radio station, when the aircraft is not expected to arrive
within plus or minus five minutes of the estimated time at
a reporting point,
the point of ADIZ entry, or
the point of destination within the ADIZ; or
within 20 nautical miles of
the estimated point of ADIZ entry, or
the centre line of the route of flight indicated in the flight plan or flight itinerary.
This section applies in respect of aircraft before entering into and while operating within Canadian domestic airspace or the ADIZ.
The pilot-in-command of an aircraft referred to in subsection (1) who is notified by an air traffic control unit of the implementation of the ESCAT Plan shall
before take-off, obtain approval for the flight from the appropriate air traffic services unit;
comply with any instruction to land or to change course or altitude that is received from the appropriate air traffic services unit; and
provide the appropriate air traffic services unit with position reports
when operating within controlled airspace, as required pursuant to section 602.125, and
when operating outside controlled airspace, at least every 30 minutes.

No person shall operate a subsonic turbo-jet aeroplane that has a maximum certificated take-off weight of 34 000 kg (74,956 pounds) or more to or from an aerodrome other than Gander International Airport unless the aeroplane meets the noise emission standards set out in Chapter 3 or 4 of Volume I, Aircraft Noise, of Annex 16 to the Convention.

aeroplane has the same meaning as in subsection 101.01(1);
maximum certificated take-off mass has the same meaning as maximum certificated take-off weight in subsection 101.01(1); and
subsonic jet has the same meaning as subsonic turbo-jet aeroplane in subsection (1).

No person shall conduct a special aviation event, other than a fly-in, unless the person complies with the provisions of a special flight operations certificate — special aviation event issued by the Minister under section 603.02.

Subject to section 6.71 of the Act, the Minister shall, on receipt of an application submitted in the form and manner required by and within the time limits specified in the Special Flight Operations Standards, issue a special flight operations certificate-special aviation event to an applicant who demonstrates to the Minister the ability to conduct a special aviation event in accordance with the Special Flight Operations Standards.
A special flight operations certificate — special aviation event shall contain the following information:
the name and address of the certificate holder;
the number of the certificate;
the date of issue of the certificate;
the validity period of the certificate;
the general conditions identified in section 603.04; and
specific conditions with respect to
the types of aircraft authorized to operate at the special aviation event and, if applicable, their registration,
the names and, if applicable, the qualifications of the flight crew members authorized to participate in the special aviation event, and
any other condition pertaining to the special aviation event that the Minister deems necessary for aviation safety.
A special flight operations certificate — special aviation event shall contain the following general conditions:
the certificate holder shall maintain an adequate management organization;
the certificate holder shall ensure that participants are
qualified for the type of demonstration to be flown, and
provided with a briefing that meets the Special Flight Operations Standards; and
the certificate holder shall conduct the special aviation event in a safe manner.
No person shall conduct a special aviation event unless the person has a management organization that
is capable of exercising supervision and operational control over
persons attending the special aviation event,
any flight that is to be operated at the special aviation event; and
personnel involved in the conduct of the special aviation event whose duties and responsibilities are specified in the Special Flight Operations Standards; and
meets the Special Flight Operations Standards.
No person shall operate an aircraft or permit an aircraft to be operated in a special aviation event unless the person operating the aircraft and the aircraft
meet the eligibility requirements specified in section 623.06 of the Special Flight Operations Standards; and
are authorized to do so in a special flight operations certificate-special aviation event.

No person shall operate an aircraft in a special aviation event at a distance from, or at an altitude above, a spectator area, a built-up area or an occupied building if that distance or altitude is less than the minimum specified in section 623.07 of the Special Flight Operations Standards.
No person shall operate an aircraft in a special aviation event in weather conditions that are below the minimum conditions specified in the Special Flight Operations Standards.
No person shall operate an aircraft in a special aviation event unless the person has received a participant briefing that meets the Special Flight Operations Standards.
This Division applies in respect of the operation of a balloon where fare-paying passengers are carried on board.

No person shall operate a balloon under this Division unless the person complies with the provisions of a special flight operations certificate — balloons issued by the Minister pursuant to section 603.18.

Subject to section 6.71 of the Act, the Minister shall, on receipt of an application submitted in the form and manner required by the Special Flight Operations Standards, issue a special flight operations certificate — balloons to an applicant who demonstrates to the Minister the ability to conduct the flight operation in accordance with the Special Flight Operations Standards.
A special flight operations certificate — balloons shall contain the following information:
the name and address of the balloon operator;
the number of the certificate;
the date of issue of the certificate;
the general conditions identified in section 603.20; and
specific conditions with respect to
the types and AX class of balloons authorized and, where the balloon is of a special shape or is a foreign-registered balloon, its registration,
the external carriage of passengers, and
any other condition pertaining to the operation that the Minister deems necessary for aviation safety.
A special flight operations certificate — balloons shall contain the following general conditions:
the balloon operator shall maintain balloons that are properly equipped for the area of operation and the type of operation;
the balloon operator shall maintain its balloons in accordance with the requirements of Subpart 5;
the balloon operator shall employ flight crew members who meet the Special Flight Operations Standards; and
the balloon operator shall conduct a safe operation.

No balloon operator shall permit a person to act and no person shall act as the pilot-in-command of a balloon unless the person meets the qualification and currency requirements set out in the Special Flight Operations Standards.
The pilot-in-command of a balloon shall ensure that passengers are given a safety briefing that meets the Special Flight Operations Standards.
No person shall operate a balloon in free flight at night unless
the balloon is equipped in accordance with section 605.19; and
landings are conducted during the day.
No person shall operate a balloon in tethered flight with passengers on board unless the pilot-in-command is on board.
The pilot-in-command shall record all time spent in tethered flight as air time for the purpose of maintenance.
No person shall operate a balloon with passengers on board unless each passenger is carried in the basket.

The following definitions apply in this Subpart.
For the purpose of interpreting a document incorporated by reference into this Subpart, unless the context requires otherwise,
“should” and “must” shall be read as “shall”;
“operator” and “aircraft operator” shall be read as “private operator”; and
“authority”, “competent aviation authority” and “operating authority” shall be read as “Minister”.
This Subpart applies to the following Canadian aircraft:
large aeroplanes;
turbine-powered aircraft;
pressurized aircraft; and
multi-engined aircraft.

Subject to subsection (2), no person shall operate any of the following Canadian aircraft for the purpose of transporting passengers or goods unless the person is the holder of a private operator registration document:
a large aeroplane;
a turbo-jet-powered aeroplane; or
a turbine-powered pressurized aeroplane certificated for more than six passenger seats.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the operation of an aircraft referred to in paragraphs (1)(a) to (c) by
an air operator who operates the aircraft in accordance with the requirements of Part VII; or
a person who operates the aircraft under a flight permit issued under section 507.04.
The applicant for a private operator registration document shall submit to the Minister an application containing the following information:
the applicant’s legal name and, if any, trade name;
the applicant’s contact information;
the names of the operations manager, chief pilot and maintenance manager;
a description of the proposed area of operation, using the chart depicted in the Index to Application of Supplementary Procedures in ICAO Document 7030, entitled Regional Supplementary Procedures;
the location of the applicant’s main base and, if any, sub-bases; and
for each aircraft that will be operated, the aircraft type, the nationality mark and the registration mark.

The Minister shall, on receipt of the application referred to in subsection (1), issue a private operator registration document to the applicant if the applicant is the registered owner of all the aircraft that will be operated under this Subpart or is permitted to use those aircraft under section 203.03.
A private operator who wishes to operate an aircraft under a special authorization shall submit to the Minister an application that
identifies the activity referred to in Division IV that the applicant wishes to carry out; and
includes a copy of the part of the private operator’s operations manual that sets out the processes, practices and procedures relating to the special authorization requested.
The Minister shall, on receipt of the application referred to in subsection (1), issue a special authorization to the applicant if the applicant
holds a private operator registration document;
is able to meet the requirements of Division IV relating to the special authorization requested; and
has an operations manual that sets out the processes, practices and procedures that are necessary to meet the requirements of Division IV relating to the special authorization requested.

A private operator shall notify the Minister if a change is made to the information contained in an application submitted under subsection 604.04(1) within ten days after the day on which the change is made.

A private operator who has been issued a special authorization, and who amends the part of the private operator’s operations manual that sets out the processes, practices and procedures relating to the special authorization, shall submit to the Minister a copy of that part of the operations manual within ten days after the day on which the amendment is made.
A private operator shall

ensure that no person is appointed operations manager or chief pilot or continues to serve as operations manager or chief pilot if, at the time of the person’s appointment or during the person’s tenure, the person has a record of conviction for
an offence under section 7.3 of the Act, or
two or more offences under these Regulations that did not arise from a single incident;

ensure that no person is appointed maintenance manager or continues to serve as maintenance manager if, at the time of the person’s appointment or during the person’s tenure, the person has a record of conviction for an offence under section 7.3 of the Act;
ensure that the operations manager performs the duties set out in section 604.204;
perform the duties set out in section 604.208; and
provide the operations manager and the maintenance manager with the financial and human resources necessary to ensure that the private operator meets the requirements of these Regulations.

No operations manager, no chief pilot and no maintenance manager shall assign to another person a management function for which he or she is responsible and accountable unless the private operator’s operations manual
identifies the functions that may be assigned;
identifies either by name or by position the persons to whom those functions may be assigned; and
describes the scope of the assignment.

The responsibility and accountability of an operations manager, a chief pilot and a maintenance manager are not affected by the assignment of a management function to another person under subsection (1).

A private operator shall have an operational control system that is adapted to the complexity of the private operator’s operations and to the private operator’s area of operation, and that meets the requirements of subsections (2) and (3).
The operational control system shall include procedures for ensuring that
all the operational requirements specified in this Subpart are met;
each aircraft is operated within the weight and balance limits specified in the aircraft flight manual;
the names of the persons on board an aircraft are recorded by the private operator before each flight; and
search and rescue authorities are notified in a timely manner if a flight is overdue or missing.
The operational control system shall include
pilot self-dispatch procedures that set out the following elements:
flight planning requirements,
the timing within which a flight crew member must inform the private operator of an aircraft’s departure and arrival, and
a method of confirming that an aircraft has arrived safely at an unattended aerodrome during a VFR flight or that an IFR flight plan has been cancelled prior to landing; or
co-authority dispatch procedures that set out the following elements:
flight planning requirements,
flight following requirements,
flight watch requirements,
a method of confirming that an aircraft has arrived safely at an unattended aerodrome during a VFR flight or that an IFR flight plan has been cancelled prior to landing,
the method by which the operational flight plan is approved and recorded by the pilot-in-command and the flight dispatcher,

if operational flight plans are prepared and accepted for a series of flights, the method by which any changes to those plans are approved and recorded by the pilot-in-command and the flight dispatcher,
if flight planning and flight watch are two separate functions, the method of switching from one to the other, and
a means to ensure that, at each location where a flight originates, the pilot-in-command will
receive meteorological information related to the flight,
receive a copy of the operational flight plan, and
can contact the responsible flight dispatcher prior to take-off.
Documentation related to the operational control of a flight shall be retained by the private operator for at least 180 days after the day on which the flight is completed.
A private operator shall designate, for each flight, a pilot-in-command or, if the crew includes two or more flight crew members, a pilot-in-command and a second-in-command.

The private operator shall record the name of the pilot-in-command and, if applicable, second-in-command designated for each flight under subsection (1) and shall retain the record for at least 180 days after the day on which the flight is completed.
A flight dispatcher and a flight follower shall, in respect of a flight conducted by a private operator,
perform flight following and flight watch;
provide any operational information requested by a flight crew member; and
notify search and rescue authorities in a timely manner if a flight is overdue or missing.

No person shall, in an aircraft operated by a private operator, conduct a landing following an instrument approach unless, immediately before landing, the pilot-in-command ascertains, by means of radiocommunication or visual inspection,
the condition of the runway or surface of intended landing; and
the wind direction and speed.

A private operator shall provide every crew member with the checklist referred to in paragraph 602.60(1)(a) or with the part of the checklist that is necessary for the performance of the crew member’s duties.
Every crew member shall follow, in the performance of his or her duties, the checklist or part of the checklist referred to in subsection (1).
A private operator may establish an aircraft operating manual for the operation of its aircraft.
An aircraft operating manual shall
contain aircraft operating procedures that are consistent with those contained in the aircraft flight manual;

contain, if the aircraft flight manual is not carried on board the aircraft, the aircraft performance data and limitations specified in that manual, and clearly identify them as aircraft flight manual requirements;
contain the private operator’s standard operating procedures, if any; and
identify the aircraft to which it relates.
No person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless an operational flight data sheet has been prepared and contains the following information:
the date of the flight;
the aircraft’s nationality mark and registration mark;
the name of the pilot-in-command;
the departure aerodrome;
the destination aerodrome;
the alternate aerodrome, if any;
the estimated flight time;
the fuel endurance;
the weight of the fuel on board the aircraft;
the zero fuel weight of the aircraft;
the take-off weight and centre of gravity of the aircraft;
the number of persons on board the aircraft;
the proposed time of departure; and
the estimated time of arrival.

The pilot-in-command of an aircraft referred to in subsection (1) shall, on the completion of each flight, record on the operational flight data sheet the flight time, time of departure, time of arrival and aerodrome of arrival.
The private operator shall retain a copy of the operational flight data sheet for at least 180 days after the day on which the flight is completed.
For the purposes of this Division, a long-range navigation system shall have the following performance capability:
the standard deviation of the lateral track deviations is less than 6.3 nautical miles;
the proportion of the total flight time that is spent by the aircraft at a distance of 30 or more nautical miles from the cleared track is less than 5.3 x 10-4; and
the proportion of the total flight time that is spent by the aircraft at a distance of 50 to 70 nautical miles from the cleared track is less than 1.3 x 10-4.

For the purposes of this Division, a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receiver is considered to be a long-range navigation system if it is installed in accordance with the requirements of Advisory Circular 20-138B, entitled Airworthiness Approval of Positioning and Navigation Systems, dated September 27, 2010 and published by the Federal Aviation Administration of the United States, as amended from time to time.

Subject to subsection (2), no person shall carry out any activity referred to in this Division or in respect of which the Minister has established requirements under subsection 604.74(1) unless that person is a private operator.
A person other than a private operator may conduct an instrument approach using a GNSS receiver to the following minima:
lateral navigation (LNAV);
lateral navigation/vertical navigation (LNAV/VNAV);
localizer performance without vertical guidance (LP); and
localizer performance with vertical guidance (LPV).

For the purposes of section 602.122, a pilot-in-command may conduct an IFR flight in an aircraft operated by a private operator when an alternate aerodrome has not been designated in the IFR flight plan or in the IFR flight itinerary if
the private operator is authorized to do so under a special authorization;
the estimated flight time is not more than six hours and the departure aerodrome is located in North America, Bermuda or the Caribbean islands;
the forecast or reported weather at the destination aerodrome, from one hour before until one hour after the estimated time of arrival, does not include
conditions, including fog or precipitation, that restrict flight visibility to less than three miles,
a thunderstorm,
a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet above the FAF altitude and a ground visibility of less than three miles,
a ceiling of less than 1,500 feet above the minimum descent altitude and a ground visibility of less than six miles, or
freezing rain, freezing drizzle or sleet;
the destination aerodrome
has at least two runways that are
operational,
separate and not reciprocal directions of the same runway, and

suitable for the aircraft on the basis of the aircraft operating procedures, the aircraft performance data and limitations specified in the aircraft flight manual, and the factors that affect the performance of the aircraft, such as atmospheric and surface conditions, and

is equipped with an emergency electrical power supply to operate the equipment and facilities that are essential for a safe landing of the aircraft in the event of a failure of the main electrical power supply; and

every flight crew member has received training, for which the validity period has not expired, in the conduct of an IFR flight when an alternate aerodrome has not been designated in the IFR flight plan or in the IFR flight itinerary.

If the requirements of paragraphs (1)(a) to (e) are met, and regardless of the departure aerodrome, the pilot-in-command of an aircraft that is operated by a private operator, and that is on a flight to a destination aerodrome in Canada, may file a new IFR flight plan or a new IFR flight itinerary that does not include an alternate aerodrome when the aircraft is within six hours’ flight time of the destination aerodrome.
Despite paragraph 602.126(1)(b),

a pilot-in-command may conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator when the reported RVR is at least 1,200 feet or the reported ground visibility is at least one quarter of a statute mile if
the private operator is authorized to do so under a special authorization,
the aircraft is operated by at least two flight crew members,
the flight plan filed for the flight specifies a take-off alternate aerodrome that

No person shall conduct an instrument procedure using a GNSS receiver in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless
the private operator is authorized to do so under a special authorization;
every flight crew member has received the following training for which the validity period has not expired:
ground training in
the GNSS and its theory of operation,
the operation of the model of GNSS receiver that will be used, and
the actions to be taken in response to GNSS receiver warnings and messages, and
in-flight training
in the operation of the model of GNSS receiver that will be used,
in the actions to be taken in response to GNSS receiver warnings and messages,
in the use of the GNSS receiver for instrument procedures and other associated duties for each crew position that the flight crew member will occupy,
provided
on board an aircraft, or

using a Level C or D full-flight simulator equipped with the same model of GNSS receiver as is installed in the private operator’s aircraft or with a model with a user interface comparable to the user interface of that GNSS receiver, and

provided by a pilot who has received training on the same model of GNSS receiver as is installed in the private operator’s aircraft or on a model with a user interface comparable to the user interface of that GNSS receiver;
every flight crew member has demonstrated to the private operator the ability to conduct an instrument approach using a GNSS receiver in accordance with this section;
the coverage area of the GNSS receiver database is compatible with the area of operation in which the aircraft will be operated;
the private operator has established procedures to ensure that
the GNSS receiver database is updated so that it remains current,
flight crew members who identify GNSS receiver database errors communicate those errors to the private operator, and
the GNSS receiver database errors identified are communicated to the private operator’s other personnel and to the GNSS receiver database provider;

if the aircraft is designed to be operated by one flight crew member, the GNSS course deviation and distance displays are located at the pilot station normally occupied by the pilot-in-command and within the primary field of vision of the flight crew member who occupies the pilot station;

if the aircraft is designed to be operated by two flight crew members, the GNSS course deviation and distance displays are located at each pilot station and within the primary field of vision of the flight crew member who occupies the pilot station;
if the aircraft is designed to be operated by one flight crew member, but can be operated by two flight crew members,
the control display unit that is linked to the GNSS receiver is centrally located in relation to the two pilot stations and provides navigation information that is visible to the pilot not flying, or
the GNSS course deviation and distance displays are located at each pilot station and within the primary field of vision of the flight crew members who occupy those pilot stations; and
the private operator has established GNSS approach procedures in order to prevent confusion between GNSS distance information and distance measuring equipment (DME) information.
No person shall conduct a CAT II or a CAT III precision approach in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless
the private operator is authorized to do so under a special authorization;
the requirements of section 602.128 are met;
every flight crew member has received, in respect of CAT II and CAT III precision approaches, ground training for which the validity period has not expired that includes the following elements:

the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of the instrument landing system (ILS), including how its performance is affected by interference from other airborne or taxiing aircraft and from ground vehicles,

the characteristics of the visual aids and the limitations on their use in reduced visibility at the various glide path angles and cockpit cut-off angles, and the height at which visual cues are expected to appear in actual operating conditions,
the operation, capabilities and limitations of the airborne systems,

the procedures and techniques for an approach, a missed approach and a rejected landing, and a description of the factors affecting height loss during a missed approach in normal and abnormal aircraft configurations,
the use and limitations of RVR, including the applicability of RVR readings from different positions along the runway,

obstacle limitation surfaces, obstacle-free zones, missed approach design criteria, obstacle clearance for a CAT II or CAT III precision approach, and obstacle clearance for a go-around and a rejected landing,
the effects of turbulence, precipitation and low level windshear,

the procedures and techniques for making the transition from instrument flight to visual flight in low RVR conditions, including the geometry of eye, wheel and antenna positions in relation to ILS reference datum height,

the actions to be taken if the required visual reference becomes inadequate when the aircraft is below the decision height, and the technique to be used for making the transition from visual flight to instrument flight if a go-around is necessary,
the actions to be taken in the event of a failure of the approach and landing equipment above and below the decision height or alert height,
the recognition of a failure of the ground equipment, and the actions to be taken in the event of such a failure,
the factors to be taken into account in the determination of the decision height or alert height,
the effect of aircraft malfunctions, including engine failure, on auto-throttle and auto-pilot performance,
the procedures to be followed and the precautions to be taken while taxiing in reduced visibility, and
the standard operating procedures to be followed by flight crew members in normal, abnormal and emergency conditions;
every flight crew member has received, in respect of CAT II and CAT III precision approaches, training on a synthetic flight training device that includes the following elements:
two approaches, at least one of which is in an engine-out configuration if the aircraft is certified under Part V to perform in that configuration,
a missed approach from the lowest minima specified in the special authorization, or a rejected landing, as applicable,
an automatic landing or a manual landing from one of the approaches, as applicable, at the maximum crosswind authorized for the aircraft, and
for CAT III approaches based on the use of a fail-passive rollout control system, a manual rollout using visual references or a combination of visual and instrument references;

every flight crew member has received, in respect of CAT II and CAT III precision approaches, training on a synthetic flight training device for which the validity period has not expired that includes the following elements:
one precision approach resulting in a landing, and
a missed approach from the lowest minima specified in the special authorization, or a rejected landing, as applicable; and
every flight crew member has demonstrated to the private operator the ability to operate the aircraft in accordance with this section.
No person shall, in an aircraft operated by a private operator, conduct an instrument procedure that is specified in the Restricted Canada Air Pilot for an aerodrome unless
the private operator is authorized to do so under a special authorization;
the person conducts the procedure in accordance with the requirements set out in the Restricted Canada Air Pilot in respect of the procedure; and

every flight crew member has received the training necessary to mitigate the risks or hazards associated with that procedure with respect to the safety of the aircraft, persons or property, and the validity period for that training has not expired.

No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated in accordance with Canadian minimum navigation performance specifications (CMNPS) or required navigation performance capability (RNPC) unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with CMNPS or RNPC;
every flight crew member has received CMNPS or RNPC training, for which the validity period has not expired, in
normal operating procedures, including long-range navigation system pre-flight data entry and periodic cross-checking of the system position display against the aircraft position,
the method of monitoring and cross-checking the long-range navigation system that is coupled to the auto-pilot,
the actions to be taken in the event of a discrepancy among long-range navigation systems, and the method of determining which is the most accurate or reliable system,
contingency procedures,
the actions to be taken in the event of a failure of one or more long-range navigation systems,
the procedure for manually updating long-range navigation systems,
airborne emergency procedures, including realignment, if applicable,
the procedure for regaining track after a deliberate or accidental deviation from the cleared track, and
RNAV systems; and
the aircraft is equipped with at least two independent long-range navigation systems or is operated as follows:
in the case of an aircraft equipped only with the radio navigation equipment referred to in paragraph 605.18(j), the aircraft is operated only on high level airways, and
in the case of an aircraft equipped with at least two independent navigation systems, one of which is a long-range navigation system, the aircraft is operated only in RNPC airspace
on high level fixed RNAV routes,
on direct routes that begin and end within the reception range of ground-based navigation aids, or
on high level airways.

No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated on a high level fixed RNAV route in accordance with required navigation performance capability (RNPC) unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with RNPC;
every flight crew member has received RNPC training, for which the validity period has not expired, in
normal operating procedures, including navigation system pre-flight data entry and periodic cross-checking of the system position display against the aircraft position,
the method of monitoring and cross-checking the navigation system that is coupled to the auto-pilot,
the actions to be taken in the event of a discrepancy among navigation systems, and the method of determining which is the most accurate or reliable system,
contingency procedures,
the actions to be taken in the event of a failure of one or more navigation systems,
the procedure for manually updating navigation systems,
airborne emergency procedures, including realignment, if applicable,
the procedure for regaining track after a deliberate or accidental deviation from the cleared track, and
RNAV systems; and
the aircraft is equipped with at least two independent navigation systems, one of which is a long-range navigation system.

No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated in accordance with North Atlantic minimum navigation performance specifications (NAT-MNPS) unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with NAT-MNPS;
every flight crew member has received NAT-MNPS training, for which the validity period has not expired, in
normal operating procedures, including long-range navigation system pre-flight data entry and periodic cross-checking of the system position display against the aircraft position,
the method of monitoring and cross-checking the long-range navigation system that is coupled to the auto-pilot,
the actions to be taken in the event of a discrepancy among long-range navigation systems, and the method of determining which is the most accurate or reliable system,
contingency procedures,
the actions to be taken in the event of a failure of one or more long-range navigation systems,
the procedure for manually updating long-range navigation systems,
airborne emergency procedures, including realignment, if applicable,
the procedure for regaining track after a deliberate or accidental deviation from the cleared track, and
RNAV systems; and

No person shall operate, in NAT-MNPS airspace, an aircraft operated by a private operator that is equipped with only one long-range navigation system, or that has only one functioning long-range navigation system, except on routes that are specified by the civil aviation authority of a contracting state as routes for aircraft equipped with only one long-range navigation system.
If the long-range navigation system referred to in subsection (2) is a GNSS receiver, it may be used if
a Canadian Technical Standard Order (CAN-TSO) design approval has been issued in respect of the GNSS receiver; or

the GNSS receiver meets the performance requirements of Technical Standard Order TSO-C196a, Airborne Supplemental Navigation Sensors for Global Positioning System Equipment Using Aircraft-Based Augmentation, published by the Federal Aviation Administration of the United States.
No person shall operate, in NAT-MNPS airspace, an aircraft operated by a private operator that is equipped only with short-range navigation equipment (VOR, DME, ADF), except on routes G3 or G11.
No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated in accordance with reduced vertical separation minima (RVSM) unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with RVSM;
every flight crew member has received RVSM training, for which the validity period has not expired, in
the floor, ceiling and horizontal boundaries of RVSM airspace,
rules on the exclusion of non-RVSM-compliant aircraft from the airspace,
the procedures to be followed by flight crew members with respect to
pre-flight and in-flight altimeter checks,
use of the automatic altitude control system,
items on the minimum equipment list,
in-flight contingencies,
weather deviation procedures,
track offset procedures for wake turbulence,
inconsequential collision-avoidance systems alerts, and
pilot level-off call,
procedures relating to non-RVSM-compliant aircraft required to carry out ferry flights, humanitarian flights or delivery flights, and
the use of an Airborne Collision Avoidance System (ACAS) and a Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS);
the aircraft meets the eligibility requirements set out in section 624.56 of Standard 624 — RVSM Eligibility Requirements, with respect to aircraft performance and aircraft equipment; and

the aircraft meets one of the following eligibility requirements:

the aircraft is equipped with the navigation equipment referred to in sections 1.3.3.1 and 1.3.3.2 of Chapter 1 of Part C of Volume II of the PBN Manual;
the equipment referred to in paragraph (d) meets the standards, criteria and functional requirements set out in sections 1.3.3.4 to 1.3.3.7 of Chapter 1 of Part C of Volume II of the PBN Manual; and

the private operator applies the processes, practices and procedures relating to the duties and practices set out in sections 1.3.4.2.1 to 1.3.4.4.4 and 1.3.6 of Chapter 1 of Part C of Volume II of the PBN Manual.
No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated in accordance with area navigation 5 (RNAV 5) requirements unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with RNAV 5 requirements;
every flight crew member has received the training referred to in paragraph 604.60(b) and the validity period for that training has not expired;
the aircraft meets one of the following eligibility requirements:

the aircraft flight manual or the pilot operating handbook, or any equivalent document provided by the manufacturer of the avionics equipment or by the aircraft manufacturer, specifies that the aircraft can be operated in accordance with RNAV 5 requirements,
the aircraft can be operated in accordance with another navigation standard with performance criteria that are equivalent to RNAV 5 requirements, or
the private operator has demonstrated to the Minister that the aircraft meets the navigational accuracy requirements for RNAV 5;
the aircraft is equipped with at least one of the position sensors referred to in section 2.3.3 of Chapter 2 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual;

the position sensors referred to in paragraph (d) meet the performance requirements, criteria and functional requirements set out in sections 2.3.3.1 to 2.3.3.3 of Chapter 2 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual; and
the private operator applies the processes, practices and procedures relating to the duties and practices set out in section 2.3.4 of Chapter 2 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual.

No person shall file a flight plan indicating that an aircraft operated by a private operator can be operated in accordance with area navigation 1 (RNAV 1) or area navigation 2 (RNAV 2) requirements unless
the private operator is authorized under a special authorization to operate the aircraft in accordance with RNAV 1 or RNAV 2 requirements;
every flight crew member has received RNAV 1 or RNAV 2 training, for which the validity period has not expired, in
pre-flight procedures for initialization, loading and verification of the area navigation system,
the normal operation of the area navigation system,
the procedure for manually updating the position of the area navigation system,
the method of monitoring and cross-checking the area navigation system,
the operation of the area navigation system in a compass unreliability area,
malfunction procedures,
terminal area procedures,
waypoint symbology, plotting procedures and record-keeping duties and practices,
timekeeping procedures,
post-flight performance checks,
flight planning,
navigation performance requirements,
enroute procedures, and
contingency procedures;
the aircraft meets one of the following eligibility requirements:

the aircraft can be operated in accordance with precision area navigation (P-RNAV) requirements based on GNSS capability under an authorization issued by the competent authority of a contracting state,

the aircraft can be operated in accordance with area navigation (RNAV) requirements based on DME/DME or DME/DME/IRU capability under an authorization issued by the Federal Aviation Administration of the United States, or

the aircraft flight manual or the pilot operating handbook, or any equivalent document provided by the manufacturer of the avionics equipment or by the aircraft manufacturer, specifies that the aircraft can be operated in accordance with RNAV 1 or RNAV 2 requirements;
the aircraft is equipped with at least one of the pieces of equipment referred to in section 3.3.3 of Chapter 3 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual;

the equipment referred to in paragraph (d) meets the performance requirements, criteria and functional requirements set out in sections 3.3.3.1 to 3.3.3.2.1.1 and 3.3.3.2.1.3 to 3.3.3.3 of Chapter 3 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual;
every flight crew member has demonstrated to the Minister the ability to operate the aircraft in accordance with this section; and

the private operator applies the processes, practices and procedures relating to the duties and practices set out in sections 3.3.3.2.1.2, 3.3.4.2 to 3.3.4.6 and 3.3.6 of Chapter 3 of Part B of Volume II of the PBN Manual.
The Minister shall establish requirements in respect of an activity that is not set out in sections 604.48 to 604.60 and in respect of which a special authorization may be issued if
the activity is subject to
operational and technical requirements established by ICAO or by the civil aviation authority of a foreign state, or

a submission to the Minister, by a private operator, an air operator or a third party, that establishes operational and technical requirements and risk mitigation measures based on an analysis of aviation-safety-related hazards;

in the case referred to in subparagraph (a)(i), the operational and technical requirements are necessary for the conduct of flights abroad or in Canada by private operators, and those flights can be conducted in a safe manner; and

in the case referred to in subparagraph (a)(ii), the operational and technical requirements and risk mitigation measures ensure the safety of the flights conducted by private operators and will not have an adverse effect on aviation safety.
If the Minister establishes requirements in respect of an activity referred to in subsection (1), no person shall, in an aircraft operated by a private operator, carry out the activity unless
the private operator is authorized to carry out the activity under a special authorization;

every flight crew member has received, if applicable, the training specified by the Minister under subsection (3) in respect of the activity, and the validity period for that training has not expired; and

every flight crew member has demonstrated to the Minister the ability to carry out the activity in accordance with the operational and technical requirements referred to in subparagraph (1)(a)(i) or (ii), as applicable, and to take the measures that are necessary to manage or mitigate the risks associated with that activity.
The Minister shall specify training in respect of an activity referred to in subsection (1) taking into account
any training that is recommended by the civil aviation authority of a foreign state or by ICAO in respect of the activity;
the risks and hazards associated with the activity with respect to the safety of the aircraft, persons or property; and
the level of safety required by the activity.
[Reserved, SOR/2015-127, s. 11]
No person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft that is operated by a private operator and that has passengers on board, move the aircraft on the surface or direct that the aircraft be moved unless

safety belts are adjusted and fastened in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(a), infants are held in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(b), and persons using child restraint systems are secured in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(c);
subject to subsection (5), seat backs are secured in the upright position;
chair tables are stowed;
carry-on baggage is stowed; and

no seat located at an emergency exit is occupied by a passenger — including a passenger who has not been informed as to how that exit operates — whose presence in that seat could adversely affect the safety of passengers or crew members during an evacuation.
No person shall conduct a landing in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless
passengers have been directed to

adjust and fasten their safety belts in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(a), hold infants in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(b), and secure persons using child restraint systems in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(c),
subject to subsection (5), secure their seat backs in the upright position,
stow their chair tables, and
stow their carry-on baggage; and

if a seat located at an emergency exit is occupied by a passenger whose presence in that seat could adversely affect the safety of passengers or crew members during an evacuation, the passenger has been directed to move to another seat.
The pilot-in-command of an aircraft operated by a private operator shall, in the event of an emergency and if time and circumstances permit,
direct passengers to

adjust and fasten their safety belts in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(a), hold infants in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(b), and secure persons using child restraint systems in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(c),
subject to subsection (5), secure their seat backs in the upright position,
stow their chair tables,
stow their carry-on baggage,
review the safety features card and assume the brace position until the aircraft stops moving, and
in the event of an emergency over water, don their life preservers; and

if a seat located at an emergency exit is occupied by a passenger whose presence in that seat could adversely affect the safety of passengers or crew members during an evacuation, direct the passenger to move to another seat.
The pilot-in-command of an aircraft operated by a private operator shall, if the “fasten safety belt” sign is turned on during the flight, direct passengers to

adjust and fasten their safety belts in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(a), hold infants in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(b), and secure persons using child restraint systems in accordance with paragraph 605.26(1)(c); and
stow their carry-on baggage.
The seat of a passenger who is certified by a physician as unable to sit upright may remain in the reclining position during movement on the surface, take-off and landing if
the passenger is not seated in a location that would restrict the evacuation of the aircraft;
the passenger is not seated in a row that is next to or immediately in front of an emergency exit; and
the seat immediately behind the passenger’s seat is vacant.
No person operating an aircraft operated by a private operator shall permit the fuelling of the aircraft while passengers are on board or are embarking or disembarking, unless

in order for persons on board the aircraft to be notified promptly of a situation that could threaten their safety, two-way communication is maintained between the ground personnel supervising the fuelling and a person on board the aircraft who has received training in emergency evacuation procedures for that aircraft type;
no ground power generator or other electrical ground power supply is being connected to or disconnected from the aircraft;
no combustion heater installed on the aircraft is being used;

every combustion heater used in the vicinity of the aircraft has a marking, applied by the manufacturer, indicating that the heater is manufactured to Canadian Standards Association (CSA) or Underwriters Laboratories of Canada (ULC) standards;

no high-energy-emitting equipment, including high-frequency radios and airborne weather radar, is being operated unless the aircraft flight manual contains procedures for its use during fuelling and those procedures are followed;
no aircraft battery is being removed or being installed;
no external battery charger is being operated or is being connected to or disconnected from an aircraft battery;
no auxiliary power unit having an efflux that discharges into the fuelling safety zone is started after filler caps are removed or fuelling connections are made;

no auxiliary power unit that is stopped is restarted until the flow of fuel has ceased, unless the aircraft flight manual establishes procedures for restarting the unit during fuelling and those procedures are followed;
no tool that is likely to produce a spark or electric arc is being used;
no photographic equipment is being used within the fuelling safety zone;
the fuelling is suspended if there is a lightning discharge within eight kilometres of the aerodrome;
the fuelling is carried out in accordance with the aircraft manufacturer’s instructions;
the aircraft emergency lighting system, if any, is armed or on;
“no smoking” signs, if any, on board the aircraft are illuminated;
no passenger is smoking or otherwise producing a source of ignition;
two exits, one of which is the door through which passengers embarked, are free of obstruction and are available for immediate use by passengers and crew members in the event of an evacuation;
the escape route from each of the exits referred to in paragraph (q) is free of obstruction and is available for immediate use by passengers and crew members in the event of an evacuation;
a person who is authorized by the private operator to suspend fuelling is on board the aircraft and is ready to direct the suspension of fuelling if a requirement of this subsection ceases to be met;
a means of evacuation is in place at the door used for the embarkation or disembarkation of passengers, is free of obstruction and is available for immediate use by passengers and crew members;
the person on board the aircraft who has received the training referred to in paragraph (a) is ready to initiate and oversee an evacuation and is at or near the door referred to in paragraph (v); and
the embarkation door is open, unless
a crew member determines that, for climatic reasons, it is desirable to close it,
a crew member is on board the aircraft, and
the door
opens inward or can be fully opened to the exterior without the need to reposition the loading stairs or stand,
is latched, if that is necessary in order to keep it closed, and
is not locked.
The person who is authorized by the private operator to suspend fuelling shall direct the suspension of fuelling if a requirement of subsection (1) ceases to be met.

For the purposes of subsection (1), fuelling safety zone means an area that extends three metres (10 feet) radially from the filling and venting points on the aircraft and from the fuelling equipment.

Despite section 602.09, a person operating an aircraft operated by a private operator may permit the fuelling of the aircraft while an engine used for the propulsion of the aircraft is running and passengers are on board or are embarking or disembarking, if
the requirements set out in subsection 604.83(1) are met;
the aircraft flight manual indicates that the engine that is running may be used as an auxiliary power unit; and
the engine that is running has a propeller brake and that brake is set.
The person who is authorized by the private operator to suspend fuelling shall direct the suspension of fuelling if a requirement of subsection (1) ceases to be met.

Despite section 602.89, no person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless passengers are given a safety briefing — orally by a crew member, or by audio or audiovisual means — that contains the following information:
when and where carry-on baggage is to be stowed;
when and how to fasten, adjust and release safety belts and, if any, shoulder harnesses;
when seat backs are to be secured in the upright position and chair tables are to be stowed;
the location of emergency exits and, in the case of a passenger seated next to such an exit, how that exit operates;
the requirement to comply with the instructions given by crew members and with the “fasten safety belt” and “no smoking” signs, and the location of those signs;
the location and operation of the passenger oxygen system, if any, including
the actions to be performed by a passenger in order to
obtain a mask,
activate the flow of oxygen, and
don and secure the mask, and
the recommendation that a passenger don and secure the passenger’s own mask before assisting another passenger with his or her mask;
the use of life preservers, including how to remove them from their packaging, how to don them and when to inflate them;
when and where smoking is prohibited;
the location of the emergency equipment required under sections 602.62, 602.63, 604.116 and 604.117, and how to access that equipment;
the portable electronic devices that may be used, and when they may be used; and
the location and purpose of the safety features card.
Despite subsection (1), a person may conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator without a safety briefing being given to the passengers if
the flight is the second or subsequent flight in a series of flights;
no additional passengers have embarked on board the aircraft; and
a crew member has verified that
carry-on baggage is stowed,
safety belts and, if any, shoulder harnesses are properly adjusted and securely fastened,
seat backs are secured in the upright position, and
chair tables are stowed.

Despite subsection (1), a person may conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator without a safety briefing being given to the passengers if each passenger on board the aircraft has, within the 12 months preceding the date of the take-off, received the information referred to in subsection (1) and training in the performance of the following actions:
fastening, adjusting and releasing safety belts and, if any, shoulder harnesses;
operating each type of floor-level exit and window emergency exit;
identifying the location of the passenger oxygen system, if any, and performing the actions necessary in order to
obtain a mask,
activate the flow of oxygen, and
don and secure the mask;
identifying the location of life preservers, if any, removing them from their packaging, donning them and inflating them; and
identifying the location of the emergency equipment required by sections 602.62, 602.63, 604.116 and 604.117 and accessing that equipment.

A private operator shall record the name of every passenger who receives the training referred to in subsection (3) and the date on which the training is received. The private operator shall retain the record for two years after the day on which the most recent entry was made.

If the safety briefing referred to in subsection (1) is insufficient for a passenger because of that passenger’s physical, sensory or comprehension limitations or because the passenger is responsible for another person on board the aircraft, the passenger shall, subject to subsection (6), be given a safety briefing that consists of
communication of the elements of the safety briefing referred to in subsection (1) that
the passenger is not able to receive either during that briefing or by referring to the safety features card, and
are necessary for the safety of the persons on board the aircraft;
communication of
the most appropriate brace position for the passenger, given the passenger’s condition, injury or stature and the orientation and pitch of his or her seat, and
where the passenger’s service animal, if any, is to be located;
in the case of a mobility-impaired passenger who would require assistance in order to move to an exit in the event of an emergency, communication of
the most appropriate exit for the passenger,
the assistance that the passenger would require to reach that exit,
the most appropriate means of providing that assistance,
the most appropriate route to that exit, and
the most appropriate time to begin to move to that exit;
in the case of a visually impaired passenger,
a tactile familiarization with
the equipment that the passenger may be required to use in the event of an emergency, and
if requested, the exits, and
communication of
where the passenger’s cane, if any, is to be stored,
the number of rows of seats separating the passenger’s seat from the closest exit and from the alternate exit, and
the features of those exits;
in the case of a passenger who is responsible for another person on board the aircraft, communication of
if the passenger is responsible for an infant,
the requirement to fasten the passenger’s safety belt and, if any, the passenger’s shoulder harness and not to secure the infant in that safety belt or shoulder harness,
how to hold the infant during take-off and landing,
how to use the child restraint system, if any,
how to place and secure the oxygen mask on the infant’s face,
the most appropriate brace position for the passenger, and
the location of the infant’s life preserver, how to remove it from its location and its packaging, how to assist the infant with donning it and when to inflate it, and
if the passenger is responsible for a person, other than an infant,
how to assist that person with donning and securing his or her oxygen mask, and
how to use that person’s personal restraint system, if any, on board the aircraft; and
in the case of an unaccompanied minor, communication of the need to pay close attention to the safety briefing.
A passenger may decline the safety briefing referred to in subsection (5).

No person shall permit passengers to disembark from an aircraft operated by a private operator unless the passengers are given a safety briefing — orally by a crew member, or by audio or audiovisual means — that contains the following information:
the safest route for passengers to take in order to move away from the aircraft; and
the hazards, if any, associated with the aircraft, including the location of Pitot tubes, propellers, rotors and engine intakes.

Subject to subsection (2), a private operator shall, before passengers on board an aircraft are given the safety briefing referred to in subsection 604.85(1), provide each passenger at his or her seat with a safety features card that shows the aircraft type and that contains safety information only in respect of the aircraft, including
in the case of an aircraft configured for 19 or fewer passenger seats,
when and how to fasten, adjust and release safety belts and, if any, shoulder harnesses,
the passenger brace position
for each type of seat and passenger restraint system, and
for a passenger who is holding an infant, and
the location, operation and use of each emergency exit, including whether it is unusable in a ditching because of the aircraft configuration,
the location and operation of the passenger oxygen system, if any, including
a description of the masks and their use,
the actions to be performed by a passenger in order to
obtain a mask,
activate the flow of oxygen, and
don and secure the mask, and
the recommendation that a passenger don and secure the passenger’s own mask before assisting another passenger with his or her mask,

the location of life preservers, how they are to be removed from their packaging, how they are to be donned by adults, by children aged two years or older and by infants, and when they are to be inflated,
when and where smoking is prohibited, and
the location, removal and use of flotation devices and, if any, life rafts; and
in the case of an aircraft configured for more than 19 passenger seats,
the information set out in subparagraphs (a)(i) to (vii),
when and where carry-on baggage is to be stowed,
the positioning of seats, securing of seat backs in the upright position and stowage of chair tables for take-off and landing,
the form, function, colour and location of the floor proximity emergency escape path markings, if any,
the safest route for passengers to take in order to move away from the aircraft in the event of an emergency, and
the attitude of the aircraft while floating, as determined by the aircraft manufacturer.

If a flight attendant is not required on board an aircraft, the safety features card referred to in subsection (1) shall also contain the information on the location of the emergency equipment required under sections 604.116, 604.117 and 604.119 and how to access that equipment.

No private operator shall assign flight time to a flight crew member, and no flight crew member shall accept such an assignment, if the flight crew member’s total flight time in all flights conducted under this Subpart, Part IV or Part VII would, as a result, exceed
1,200 hours in a period of 12 consecutive months;
300 hours in a period of 90 consecutive days;
120 hours in a period of 30 consecutive days; or
8 hours in a period of 24 consecutive hours, if the assignment is for a single-pilot IFR flight.

If a flight crew’s flight duty period is extended under section 604.101, each flight crew member accumulates, for the purposes of subsection (1), the total flight time for the flight or the total flight time for the series of flights, as the case may be.

Subject to sections 604.100 to 604.102, no private operator shall assign flight duty period to a flight crew member, and no flight crew member shall accept such an assignment, if the flight crew member’s flight duty period would, as a result, exceed
14 consecutive hours in a period of 24 consecutive hours; or
15 consecutive hours in a period of 24 consecutive hours, if
the flight crew member’s total flight duty period in the previous 30 consecutive days does not exceed 70 hours, or
the rest period before the flight is at least 24 hours.
A private operator shall ensure that, prior to reporting for flight duty, a flight crew member is provided with the minimum rest period and with any additional rest period required by this Division.
A flight crew member shall use the following periods to be adequately rested prior to reporting for flight duty:
the minimum rest period provided under subsection (2);
any additional rest period required by this Division; and
any period with no assigned duties provided under section 604.104.
Flight duty period may be extended by one half of the length of the rest period, to a maximum of four hours, if

before a flight crew member reports for the first flight or reports as a flight crew member on standby, as the case may be, the private operator provides the flight crew member with notice of the extension of the flight duty period;
the private operator provides the flight crew member with a rest period of at least four consecutive hours in suitable accommodation; and
the flight crew member’s next minimum rest period is increased by an amount of time at least equal to the length of the extension of the flight duty period.

If a flight crew is augmented by at least one flight crew member, if there is a balanced distribution of flight deck duty time and rest periods among the flight crew members, and if the next minimum rest period is at least equal to the length of the preceding flight duty period, the flight crew’s flight duty period may be extended
to 17 hours with a maximum flight deck duty time of 12 hours, if a flight relief facility — seat is provided; and
to 20 hours with a maximum flight deck duty time of 14 hours, if a flight relief facility — bunk is provided.
Flight duty period may be extended by up to three hours if
the pilot-in-command, after consultation with the other flight crew members, considers it safe to do so;
the flight duty period is extended as a result of an unforeseen operational circumstance that occurs after the beginning of the flight duty period;
the next minimum rest period is extended by an amount of time that is at least equal to the length of the extension of the flight duty period; and
the pilot-in-command notifies the private operator of the unforeseen operational circumstances and of the length of the extension of the flight duty period.
The private operator shall retain a copy of the notification for five years.

When a private operator delays a flight crew member’s reporting time by more than three hours, the flight crew member’s flight duty period is considered to start three hours after the original reporting time if the private operator notifies the flight crew member of the delay
within 12 hours before the original reporting time; and
at least one hour before the flight crew member leaves a rest facility.

No private operator shall assign duties to a flight crew member, and no flight crew member shall accept those duties, unless the private operator provides the flight crew member with one of the following periods with no assigned duties:
at least 36 consecutive hours in a period of seven consecutive days; or
at least three consecutive calendar days in a period of 17 consecutive days.

If a flight crew member is required by a private operator to travel for the purpose of positioning after the completion of flight duty period, the private operator shall provide the flight crew member with an additional rest period that is at least equal to one half of the time spent for that purpose that is in excess of the flight duty period referred to in paragraphs 604.99(1)(a) and (b).
No private operator shall allow a flight crew member to take a controlled rest on the flight deck of an aircraft operated by the private operator unless
the private operator has a controlled-rest-on-the-flight-deck program that includes the following elements:
guidelines on the use of controlled rest, including the factors allowing or preventing its use,
the general principles relating to fatigue and fatigue countermeasures, and
the procedures to be followed by participating crew members before, during and after a controlled rest; and
every participating crew member has received training relating to the elements of the controlled-rest-on-the-flight-deck program.

The pilot-in-command of an aircraft operated by a private operator shall determine whether the flight conditions, the duration of the flight and the physiological condition of the crew members allow a controlled rest on the flight deck to be taken by a flight crew member.
The pilot-in-command of an aircraft operated by a private operator shall give participating crew members a briefing that includes the following elements:
the order in which the periods of controlled rest are to be taken by the flight crew members;
the planned duration of each period of controlled rest;
the circumstances under which a resting flight crew member is to be woken;
the procedures for the transfer of flight controls and duties; and
flight attendant duties in relation to a controlled rest.
The flight crew members on board an aircraft operated by a private operator shall
prior to each controlled rest on the flight deck,
participate in an operational briefing,
carry out the transfer of duties, and
inform the flight attendants of the controlled rest; and
remain on the flight deck during the controlled rest.
The flight crew member who supervises a controlled rest on the flight deck of an aircraft operated by a private operator shall, during the controlled rest,
perform the duties of the resting flight crew member;
ensure that the controlled rest is taken only during the cruise portion of the flight and is completed at least 30 minutes before top of descent;
ensure that the period of controlled rest is of no more than 45 minutes in duration;
ensure that the resting flight crew member is awake for at least 15 minutes before the resumption of duties, except in abnormal or emergency conditions; and
after the completion of the controlled rest, give an operational briefing to the flight crew member who has taken the controlled rest.
For the purposes of this section, participating crew member means the resting flight crew member and the flight crew member who supervises the controlled rest on the flight deck.

No person shall operate an aircraft operated by a private operator, other than an aircraft referred to in subsection 602.61(2), unless a survival manual is carried on board that contains information about how to use the survival equipment that is carried on board to meet the requirements of subsection 602.61(1).

No person shall operate an aircraft operated by a private operator on board of which life rafts are required to be carried in accordance with section 602.63 unless the survival kit referred to in paragraph 602.63(6)(c) contains
a life raft repair kit;
a bailing bucket and a sponge;
a whistle;
a waterproof flashlight;

a supply of potable water — based on 500 mL per person and calculated using the rated capacity of the life raft — or a means of desalting or distilling salt water that can provide 500 mL of potable water per person;
a waterproof survival manual that contains information about how to use the survival equipment;
a first aid kit that contains antiseptic swabs, burn dressing compresses, bandages and motion sickness pills; and

a pyrotechnic signalling device, or an aviation visual distress signal that has a marking applied by the manufacturer indicating that the signal meets the requirements of CAN-TSO-C168, a signalling mirror and a dye marker for visually signalling distress.
Despite subsection (2), if there is insufficient space in the attached survival kit, a supplemental survival kit shall be stowed adjacent to each required life raft and contain

a supply of potable water — based on 500 mL per person and calculated using the rated capacity of the life raft — or a means of desalting or distilling salt water that can provide 500 mL of potable water per person; and
motion sickness pills.

No person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator that is configured as follows unless, for the purposes of paragraph 602.60(1)(h), the corresponding number of first aid kits is carried on board and each kit contains the supplies and equipment set out in the Aviation Occupational Health and Safety Regulations:
configured for 0 to 50 passenger seats, one kit;
configured for 51 to 150 passenger seats, two kits;
configured for 151 to 250 passenger seats, three kits; and
configured for 251 or more passenger seats, four kits.
No person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless
the first aid kits referred to in subsection (1) are distributed throughout the cabin and are readily available to crew members and passengers;
each first aid kit is clearly identified; and
if a first aid kit is stowed in a bin or compartment, the bin or compartment is clearly marked as containing a first aid kit.

No person shall conduct a take-off in a pressurized aircraft operated by a private operator that has flight attendants on board unless one unit of protective breathing equipment with a 15-minute portable supply of breathing gas at a pressure-altitude of 8,000 feet is available
at the entry into each Class A, B, E and F cargo compartment accessible to crew members during flight;
at the site of each hand-held fire extinguisher that is located in an isolated galley;
on the flight deck; and
at the site of each hand-held fire extinguisher that is required under section 604.119.

If the breathing gas in the protective breathing equipment referred to in subsection (1) is oxygen, each unit of that equipment reduces by 15 minutes the crew member oxygen requirements specified in subsection 605.31(2).
No person shall conduct a take-off in an aircraft operated by a private operator unless
hand-held fire extinguishers are available as follows:
extinguishers are distributed, in every passenger compartment configured as follows, in the numbers indicated:
in a passenger compartment configured for fewer than 20 passenger seats, one extinguisher,
in a passenger compartment configured for 20 to 60 passenger seats, two extinguishers,
in a passenger compartment configured for 61 to 200 passenger seats, three extinguishers, and
in a passenger compartment configured for 201 or more passenger seats, one additional extinguisher for each additional unit of 100 passenger seats,
one extinguisher is located at the entrance to each Class E cargo compartment that is accessible to crew members during flight, and
one extinguisher is located in each isolated galley; and
if a hand-held fire extinguisher is stowed in a bin or compartment, the bin or compartment is clearly marked as containing a fire extinguisher.
The maintenance manager is responsible and accountable for the maintenance control system.
A private operator shall have, in respect of its aircraft, a maintenance control system that includes

in the case of a private operator who provides the parts and materials that will be used in the performance of maintenance or elementary work, procedures to ensure that only parts and materials that meet the requirements of Subpart 71 of Part V are used, including
the details of part pooling arrangements, if any, that have been entered into by the private operator, and
procedures used for the inspection and storage of incoming parts and materials;
